children.name: Today we are splitting Ghostty's core into a library. The app you run keeps its window, its fonts and its configuration; the terminal underneath becomes something another program can embed.

The surface is deliberately small. A host hands libghostty a native surface and a size, and gets back a grid of cells it can draw however it likes. Input arrives as an event queue, not as callbacks into the host's event loop.
What does not change: the parser, the renderer's cell model, and the escape-sequence coverage. What does: everything that used to assume it owned a window.
libghostty splits Ghostty's core out of the app so other frontends can embed the terminal without the macOS shell.
The ABI is deliberately narrow: a surface, a grid of cells and an input queue, with no windowing or font policy in the library.
Commenters split on whether a stable C ABI is worth the loss of Zig's comptime ergonomics inside the core.
Tab selects a citation  ·  Enter reads its source
The interesting part is what they left out. No windowing, no font stack, no config language — those all stay in the app. That is the whole reason this can be embedded.
I have wanted this for years. Every terminal library I have tried eventually grows its own opinion about how a window should look.
A narrow ABI is great until you need one more callback. Then you version the struct and every embedder has to care.
Does the host get to choose the font, or does the library still own the cell grid? That is the line I keep tripping over when I try to imagine embedding this in a browser.
Related from 2024: the original libghostty design notes. The section on input is the one worth reading first.

Author here. Happy to answer questions about the ABI, but the design notes cover most of what people are asking.
